extracted.intended_audience: story-writers, students of short fiction, and readers/students of American literature
extracted.subtask_description: Reading an editor's anthology (1915–1939) to learn what makes American short stories effective: representativeness, craft features (voice, economy, characterization), and historical development. Useful for writers and students analyzing technique and selection criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative selection / panoramic picture
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the stories which are "most representative in their distinction" and thus present "a panoramic picture of the period."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor states he selected fifty stories published during the past twenty-five years that are 'most representative in their distinction' to allow readers to 'watch the progress of the American short story' and to give a 'tolerably satisfactory portrait of the changes in mood and manners' during the period. Use representativeness across time, mood, and manners as a selection criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolution beyond simple narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: The short story has moved from being 'simply narrative harking back to English models' to aiming 'at rather more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate stories for ambition beyond mere plot/narration—the degree to which they aim for deeper effect, form, or insight rather than just telling an incident in a conventional narrative way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture and transfer of ordinary mood
rubrics_metrics.description: "America has learned to surprise the mood on the face of the man next door and to transfer it innocently to paper so that it tells us something we need to know about ourselves."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong short story often observes and renders everyday moments, gestures, or moods in a way that reveals wider truths about character or society. Look for truthful small moments that illuminate larger human or social realities (editorial formulation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dependence on a contrived surprise ending
rubrics_metrics.description: "The short story, like life, can seldom be shocked into a sudden surprise ending."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories should not rely primarily on an artificial twist. Prefer endings that grow organically from character and situation rather than a forced shock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground morphology/technique in life
rubrics_metrics.description: "The morphology which the student has to learn, but anything the student learns in this respect he must learn from life."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students and writers should learn structure and form from observing life; authentic detail and lived experience should inform technique and story morphology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dignity and substance of prose
rubrics_metrics.description: American writing in the period 'has achieved dignity and substance as a rich literature in its own right.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value writing that attains seriousness and depth—prose with weight, clarity, and substantive thematic or emotional content rather than mere cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect implication to create effects
rubrics_metrics.description: William Faulkner 'excels at creating his effects by indirect implication.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how a story communicates truth or atmosphere indirectly—through implication, suggestion, and oblique detail—rather than explicit statement. Consider Faulkner's use of implication to convey familial or social truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey truth through limited/child perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Faulkner's That Evening Sun Go Down 'conveys to us the truth about a family through the half-unrealized perceptions of the children who witness the events.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how viewpoint—especially limited or child perspectives—can reveal larger realities indirectly via perception, misunderstanding, or partial knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and understatement
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuel Komroff's work is noted for 'economy and understatement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value tight, economical prose and restrained presentation; understatement can be a strength when it implies more than it states outright (Komroff, Napoleon's Hat Under Glass as example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic approach / poetic treatment of reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Several writers (Komroff, Alan Marshall) are praised for a 'poetic approach to reality' or 'cloaking simple realism with a poetic treatment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the extent to which realist material is rendered with poetic language, lyricism, or metaphor—balancing factual detail with poetic sensitivity to enhance effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy combined with fantasy/lightness
rubrics_metrics.description: Komroff's writing shows 'light and fantastic treatment of themes' and a 'poetic approach to reality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize stories that blend concise storytelling with elements of fantasy or the fantastic, using lightness to touch reality evocatively (Komroff influenced by Maupassant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization and ear for speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise for 'brilliant talents for characterization and a fine ear for folk speech' (George Albee) and similar notes elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the vividness, complexity, and consistency of characters, and the authenticity of dialogue and dialect; a strong ear for speech can ground characterization and setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographic realism and quick ear for speech
rubrics_metrics.description: James T. Farrell: 'photographic realism and quick ear for speech.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess fidelity to physical and social detail (realism) combined with authentic dialogue; realism can be 'photographic' in immediacy while still serving thematic ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartial presentation and behaviorist psychological attitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Erskine Caldwell's stories noted for 'impartial presentation of poor-white life' and a 'psychological attitude behaviorist.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value an observational, unsentimental stance that presents characters' actions and circumstances without heavy authorial judgment; consider how behavior is shown rather than explained psychologically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incisiveness and relative impersonality
rubrics_metrics.description: Kay Boyle: 'often been compared to Katherine Mansfield... have a similar incisiveness. Kay Boyle is more impersonal than Katherine Mansfield.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for sharp, penetrating insights (incisiveness) and a tone that may favor impersonal observation over intimate subjectivity when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stream-of-consciousness technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Tess Slesinger 'is the most successful American short-story writer using the stream-of-consciousness technique.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate mastery of interior monologue/flow-of-thought presentation: coherence, voice, and whether the technique serves characterization and theme rather than self-indulgence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventiveness / form invention
rubrics_metrics.description: William Saroyan 'has invented a new form successfully for the short story.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reward formal experimentation and successful invention of new narrative techniques or structures that expand what a short story can do.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social consciousness / social critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Albert Maltz 'embodied the growing social consciousness of our time in better stories'; Fitzgerald is noted as a social critic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how stories engage social issues, critique social conditions, or embody a conscious social perspective; social engagement can be a core value in selection and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of sentiment; avoid excess
rubrics_metrics.description: Robert Whitehand's American Nocturne 'might easily have failed through excess of sentiment, but as it stands it is nearly faultless.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate emotional restraint and the author's control over sentiment; excessive sentimentality weakens effect, while disciplined feeling can strengthen it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustained narrative effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Lovell Thompson's story 'This sustained effort in the vein of Joseph Conrad is an unforgettable story.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value stories that maintain tone, tension, and craft across a sustained narrative stretch; consider stamina and unity of purpose in longer or more ambitious short pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relentless inevitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Pietro di Donato's Christ in Concrete praised for 'relentless inevitability.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether events and consequences in the story feel inevitable and tightly causal—an inexorable logic that reinforces tragic or thematic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delicate idyl and near-faultless control
rubrics_metrics.description: Robert Whitehand's 'delicate idyl' that could have failed from excess but is 'nearly faultless.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize skillful handling of delicate, lyrical material where fine control prevents sentiment or sentimentality from undermining the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warm-blooded, richly human tone and vitality
rubrics_metrics.description: Peter Neagoe's Rumanian peasant tales are 'warm-blooded, richly human, and full of a riotous pagan zest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value vitality, human warmth, and exuberant life in storytelling; expressive warmth can make character and culture vividly present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dialogue for pathetically humorous effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Dorothy M'Cleary 'has a gift for pathetically humorous dialogue and her characterization is excellent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the interplay of pathos and humor in dialogue; dialogue that mixes poignancy and comedy can deepen reader engagement and reveal character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection emphasis on works that teach writers
rubrics_metrics.description: Editor: 'If you are a story-writer, that will be one of your best lessons... Suppose you watch them grow.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use selected stories as models to learn craft—study progression, techniques, and contrasts between earlier and later stories to learn how the short story develops.
